The folder `data/` holds the data behind a published data story, "The Structure of Stand-Up Comedy": https://pudding.cool/2018/02/stand-up
The files: data/ali-wong--captions.csv, data/ali-wong--topics.csv

Write down the story's findings that this data reproduces.

1. Read the story on the web. web_fetch returns the page as the server sends it. web_view opens it in a browser and scrolls it like a reader, so it also gets text drawn by scripts, chart labels and the text of scrolling steps: use it when web_fetch returns little of the story, and to read what the charts label. Follow links to the story's methods or data notes when they say how a number was computed.
2. List every finding the authors draw from data: each number, comparison, ranking, share, trend or pattern the text states or a chart labels. A description of the data itself is not a finding: how many records, people, items, categories or sources it has, and how it was collected. When a chart states the same thing for each of its items (the top three for each phrase, the share for each year), that is one finding, written as one fact whose code computes it for every item at once.
3. Write each finding the files in data/ can reproduce as a fact in `facts.json`:

```json
[{"id": "women-front-shorter",
  "source": "On average, the pockets in women's jeans are 48% shorter and 6.5% narrower than men's pockets.",
  "claim": "Women's front pockets average 14.3 cm of maximum height against 23.1 cm for men.",
  "tables": {"m": "data/measurements.csv"},
  "code": "m.groupby('menWomen').maxHeightFront.mean()"}]
```

- `id`: unique in the file, a few meaningful words.
- `source`: the story's own words for this finding, quoted exactly, from its text or a chart label.
- `claim`: the finding in one sentence, with the numbers the code prints, and nothing the printout does not show: the story's own wording and numbers belong in `source`, not in the claim.
- `tables`: the files the code reads, each a variable name and the file's path from this folder, such as `data/orders.csv`; every file is read with `pd.read_csv(path)`.
- `code`: one Python expression over those variables, with `pd` (pandas) and `np` (numpy) available: the plain pandas computation whose printout shows the finding, such as a filter, a group-by, a count, a share or a sort. Do not assemble the result into a hand-made Series or dict.

Evaluate every fact from this folder the way it will be checked: read its `tables` with `pd.read_csv`, evaluate its `code`, print the value the way pandas prints it, and read the printout against the claim and the source. Every number, name and comparison in the claim must be in the printout, computed from the tables: code that writes a number itself, such as a string or a Series of typed-in values, does not count. The printout must agree with the story's numbers, up to rounding. Use the story's own definitions and filters, from its text or methods: a term means the same in every fact (if making it past the rookie contract is more than two seasons in one fact, it is more than two seasons in all of them), and a range, threshold or subset is one the story uses, never one chosen to make a number come out right. If the story's number only comes out under a definition or filter the story does not use, the finding is not reproduced. If after a fair try the data does not give the story's number (it needs other data, a different period, or the numbers differ beyond rounding), leave the finding out of facts.json.

4. Write `skipped.json`: every finding you left out, as [{"source": "the story's words", "why": "..."}].

Deliver both files, even when the data reproduces none of the story's findings: then `facts.json` is `[]`.
I'll start by exploring the data files and reading the story.

Here is every line from Ali Wong’s stand-up comedy special, Baby
Cobra .
We’re going to explain why her hour-long routine is so great.
But first, know
that you can tap on the right to skip forward. Try it! you can click on the right to skip forward. Or use the keyboard. < >
Nice! Ok, back to Ali Wong’s comedy special...
We noticed something special about 50 minutes into the show.
Each marks noticeable audience laughter. The circle size
denotes how long the audience laughed.
In fact, this moment had the most laughter in the entire
show. We’ll call it the “laughter climax.”
Why was this moment so funny? After dissecting it, we’re going to show you how
form—the structure of the entire routine—played a big role. Form made the joke
funnier.
We discovered this when we set out to understand the laughter climax.
First, we looked for the beginning of the story that triggered it. With its
starting point, we could see how the story developed into the biggest laugh.
The laughter climax is about conception. We worked our way
backward to see how she arrived at that topic.
The punchline about conception was preceded by a reference
to being a hippy, which was preceded by a description of a man’s face during orgasm.
We kept working backward, and we ended up slicing the entire routine into
self-contained topics, yielding a map of all subject matter in the comedy special.
Yet when looking at the entire routine, we noticed that some of these topics
weren’t so separate. For example, let’s examine the first three minutes of the show.
She has a whole digression about HPV that’s divided into three parts: everyone has it, men don’t get it, and Ali’s experience at the doctor.
But the reason she got to the topic of HPV was because of her difficulty falling asleep.
And the reason she is talking about falling asleep: she’s jealous of other women who can fall asleep, as well as their metabolism and inner thigh clearance.
Generally, a comedian’s stories will flow from one to another, but there’s often no
collective “point” The outcome of an hour-long stand-up routine is different from other long-form
compositions (e.g., films, books, plays).
But if you take a step back, Ali’s routine is structured around three cohesive
ideas: getting older, marriage, and pregnancy.
Let’s put this into context. If you’re studying theatre, literature, or film, you
make sense of the work by breaking down its plot or form.
In film, for example, the smallest, irreducible unit is the “beat,” described by
screenwriting instructor Robert McKee as “an exchange of behavior in action/reaction.”
Those small pieces—the beats—build a scene...
...and scenes build an act. We analyze the division and subdivision of a story to
understand what it’s about.
And we find that we can do this with Ali Wong’s routine. Unlike some stand-up, it
adds up into something bigger. She’s telling not just 100 individual jokes, but a story that is
deliberately arranged, much like a comedy film or a TV series.
We can think of comedy as a spectrum, from one-line jokes to a feature film.
As we move from left to right, we have more topic continuity and use of structure.
The humor requires and builds off of context.
Ali Wong’s stand-up is closer to the right of this spectrum, relying less on
one-liners and more on form-driven humor. It helps makes her routine great, and the jokes hit for
different reasons than we sometimes expect in stand-up. The laughter climax is one example of this.
Let’s zoom in again on the laughter climax to see
why.
We can tie this punchline to a larger three-minute story about making babies.
It also “calls back” to three other topics from earlier in the routine.
The laughter climax is meta funny. For 50 minutes, Ali has built a
universe, with each joke expanding the audience’s understanding of her world-view.
The laughter climax connects the major themes of her routine, from how she met her husband to her philosophy on
working. When the punchline hits, the seemingly disparate stories snap together.
You get the same feeling when reaching the end of a great Seinfeld episode or any
multi-plot story—the delight in seeing all the plotlines converge into one (and realizing that the
storyteller was crafting a deeper idea all along).
Screenwriting educator Robert McKee devotes a large part of teaching
to story structure. Screenwriting is not about the exact words said (i.e., the jokes) but the pattern of
events and the meaning behind them. For example, here’s a point about structure that he makes in
screenwriting bible Story ...
“If, however, we were to put the content of their films aside for the moment, and
study the pure patterning of their events, we’d see that, like a melody without a lyric, like a silhouette
without a matrix, their story designs are powerfully charged with meaning.”
“Stripped of its surface of
characterization and location, story structure reveals his personal insight into the deepest patterns and
motivations for how and why things happen in this world––his map of life’s hidden order.”
This is what we get when stand-up isn’t just joke after joke after joke.
The structure of her routine leaves us with something more, much like a film short
or a play would. Her hour-long show is different because we see her world-view. We understand her
experience being pregnant.
We learn Ali’s “map of life’s hidden order.”
?

format, individually annotated the entire routine, then collectively reviewed and merged into a single data
set. Title art by Jason Wong . Get in touch:
russell@polygraph.cool / Russell or
matt@polygraph.cool / Matt .

Here is every line from Ali Wong’s stand-up comedy special, _Baby Cobra_.
We’re going to explain why her hour-long routine is so great.
But first, know that you can tap on the right to skip forward. Try it! you can click on the right to skip forward. Or use the keyboard.<>
Nice! Ok, back to Ali Wong’s comedy special...
We noticed something special about 50 minutes into the show.
Each marks noticeable audience laughter. The circle size denotes how long the audience laughed.
In fact, this moment had the most laughter in the entire show. We’ll call it the “laughter climax.”
Why was this moment so funny? After dissecting it, we’re going to show you how form—the structure of the entire routine—played a big role. Form made the joke funnier.
We discovered this when we set out to understand the laughter climax.
First, we looked for the beginning of the story that triggered it. With its starting point, we could see how the story developed into the biggest laugh.
The laughter climax is about conception. We worked our way backward to see how she arrived at that topic.
The punchline about conception was preceded by a reference to being a hippy, which was preceded by a description of a man’s face during orgasm.
We kept working backward, and we ended up slicing the entire routine into self-contained topics, yielding a map of all subject matter in the comedy special.
Yet when looking at the entire routine, we noticed that some of these topics weren’t so separate. For example, let’s examine the first three minutes of the show.
She has a whole digression about HPV that’s divided into three parts: everyone has it,men don’t get it, and Ali’s experience at the doctor.
But the reason she got to the topic of HPV was because of her difficulty falling asleep.
And the reason she is talking about falling asleep: she’s jealous of other women who can fall asleep, as well as their metabolism and inner thigh clearance.
Generally, a comedian’s stories will flow from one to another, but there’s often no collective “point” The outcome of an hour-long stand-up routine is different from other long-form compositions (e.g., films, books, plays).
But if you take a step back, Ali’s routine is structured around three cohesive ideas: getting older,marriage, and pregnancy.
Let’s put this into context. If you’re studying theatre, literature, or film, you make sense of the work by breaking down its plot or form.
In film, for example, the smallest, irreducible unit is the “beat,” described by screenwriting instructor Robert McKee as “an exchange of behavior in action/reaction.”
Those small pieces—the beats—build a scene...
...and scenes build an act. We analyze the division and subdivision of a story to understand what it’s about.
And we find that we can do this with Ali Wong’s routine. Unlike some stand-up, it adds up into something bigger. She’s telling not just 100 individual jokes, but a story that is deliberately arranged, much like a comedy film or a TV series.
We can think of comedy as a spectrum, from one-line jokes to a feature film.
As we move from left to right, we have more topic continuity and use of structure. The humor requires and builds off of context.
Ali Wong’s stand-up is closer to the right of this spectrum, relying less on one-liners and more on form-driven humor. It helps makes her routine great, and the jokes hit for different reasons than we sometimes expect in stand-up. The laughter climax is one example of this.
Let’s zoom in again on the laughter climax to see why.
We can tie this punchline to a larger three-minute story about making babies.
It also “calls back” to three other topics from earlier in the routine.
The laughter climax is meta funny. For 50 minutes, Ali has built a universe, with each joke expanding the audience’s understanding of her world-view.
The laughter climax connects the major themes of her routine, from how she met her husband to her philosophy on working. When the punchline hits, the seemingly disparate stories snap together.
You get the same feeling when reaching the end of a great Seinfeld episode or any multi-plot story—the delight in seeing all the plotlines converge into one (and realizing that the storyteller was crafting a deeper idea all along).
Screenwriting educator Robert McKee devotes a large part of teaching to story structure. Screenwriting is not about the exact words said (i.e., the jokes) but the pattern of events and the meaning behind them. For example, here’s a point about structure that he makes in screenwriting bible _Story_...
“If, however, we were to put the content of their films aside for the moment, and study the pure patterning of their events, we’d see that, like a melody without a lyric, like a silhouette without a matrix, their story designs are powerfully charged with meaning.”
“Stripped of its surface of characterization and location, story structure reveals his personal insight into the deepest patterns and motivations for how and why things happen in this world––his map of life’s hidden order.”
This is what we get when stand-up isn’t just joke after joke after joke.
The structure of her routine leaves us with something more, much like a film short or a play would. Her hour-long show is different because we see her world-view. We understand her experience being pregnant.
We learn Ali’s “map of life’s hidden order.”

That's 6, of which 3 are real themes. But how compute "three cohesive ideas"? Maybe the three level-1 groups with the longest duration. Let's compute durations of level-1 topic spans.

Actually topics file: each row is a topic node, timeStart/totalStop. Level 1 rows: 
- 0-intro 28-49
- 6-getting older 49-62 (then 398-410), totalStop 410
- 96-marriage 415-442 totalStop 2255 (and 1766-1777)
- 599-paintball 2258-2268
- 601-pregnancy 2277-2285 totalStop 3437 (and 2645-2654)
- 904-conclusion 3442-3465

So top-level themes and durations: getting older = 410-49 = 361s; marriage = 2255-415 = 1840s; pregnancy = 3437-2277 = 1160s; intro 21; paintball 10; conclusion 23.

Hmm total 3535.

The story says "structured around three cohesive ideas: getting older, marriage, and pregnancy". That's exactly the three level-1 topics besides wrapper ones, but a code needs to select them: maybe level==1 & totalStop-timeStart > some? Not story's filter. Could just print level-1 groups with their spans, showing those three dominate. But claim "three cohesive ideas" is a qualitative finding. We could compute the count of level-1 groups excluding intro/conclusion? That's choosing filter.

Alternatively the story's "three cohesive ideas" is drawn from topics at level 1: getting older, marriage, pregnancy. The three longest at level 1. A fact could be: the three longest top-level topics are marriage (1840s), pregnancy (1160s), getting older (361s). Code: group level-1 by group, compute max totalStop - min timeStart, sort top 3. Hmm.

But what chart labels does the story have? I should try harder to see them. Maybe use web_view with a larger viewport/scroll through all steps. web_view output was cut at the end of article (?) It showed the "?" before methodology. It didn't show any chart values. Perhaps the story has no chart-axis numbers at all; visuals are transcripts. The text states: "50 minutes", "most laughter in the entire show", "three parts", "three cohesive ideas", "100 individual jokes", "three-minute story", "three other topics", "first three minutes". Also "For 50 minutes, Ali has built a universe". These are findings.

Maybe the story includes an interactive chart with a y-axis of "laughs per minute" and labels. Did web_view capture chart labels? It captured "Each [circle] marks noticeable audience laughter." Maybe the circle is a unicode char rendered. The transcript lines themselves are the chart.

I recall the visual: it's a horizontal "comedy special" transcript, with each line's width proportional to time, and vertical bars for laughter, colored by topic; on scroll it zooms. There might not be axis labels with numbers.

Let me try to find the source via GitHub search from the browser jina on github search page. https://r.jina.ai/https://github.com/search?q=... Maybe GitHub search requires login but public code search? Try.

Also the Pudding's repos: I know they publish on GitHub under "the-pudding" e.g., "the-pudding/stand-up" might exist. 						 Here is every line from Ali Wong’s stand-up comedy special, Baby
								Cobra . 
					

				

				 
					 
						 We’re going to explain why her hour-long routine is so great.
But first, know
							that you can tap on the right to skip forward. Try it! you can click on the right to skip forward. Or use the keyboard. < > 
					

				

				 
					 
						 Nice! Ok, back to Ali Wong’s comedy special... 
					

				

				 
					 
						 We noticed something special about 50 minutes into the show. 
					

				

				 
					 
						 Each marks noticeable audience laughter. The circle size
							denotes how long the audience laughed. 
					

				

				 
					 
						 In fact, this moment had the most laughter in the entire
							show. We’ll call it the “laughter climax.” 
					

				

				 
					 
						 Why was this moment so funny? After dissecting it, we’re going to show you how
							form—the structure of the entire routine—played a big role. Form made the joke
								funnier. 
					

				

				 
					 
						 We discovered this when we set out to understand the laughter climax. 
					

				

				 
					 
						 First, we looked for the beginning of the story that triggered it. With its
							starting point, we could see how the story developed into the biggest laugh. 
					

				

				 
					 
						 The laughter climax is about conception. We worked our way
							backward to see how she arrived at that topic. 
					

				

				 
					 
						 The punchline about conception was preceded by a reference
							to being a hippy, 
	 
	 
 which was preceded by a description of a man’s face during orgasm. 
	 
	 
 
					

				

				 
					 
						 We kept working backward, and we ended up slicing the entire routine into
							self-contained topics, yielding a map of all subject matter in the comedy special. 
					

				

				 
					 
						 Yet when looking at the entire routine, we noticed that some of these topics
							weren’t so separate. For example, let’s examine the first three minutes of the show. 
					

				

				 
					 
						 She has a whole digression about HPV that’s divided into three parts: everyone has it, 
	 
	 
 men don’t get it, and Ali’s experience at the doctor. 
					

				

				 
					 
						 But the reason she got to the topic of HPV was because of her difficulty falling asleep. 
					

				

				 
					 
						 And the reason she is talking about falling asleep: she’s jealous of other women who can fall asleep, as well as their metabolism 
	 
	 
 and inner thigh clearance. 
					

				

				 
					 
						 Generally, a comedian’s stories will flow from one to another, but there’s often no
							collective “point” The outcome of an hour-long stand-up routine is different from other long-form
							compositions (e.g., films, books, plays). 
					

				

				 
					 
						 But if you take a step back, Ali’s routine is structured around three cohesive
							ideas: getting older, marriage, and pregnancy. 
					

				

				 
					 
						 Let’s put this into context. If you’re studying theatre, literature, or film, you
							make sense of the work by breaking down its plot or form. 
					

				

				 
					 
						 In film, for example, the smallest, irreducible unit is the “beat,” described by
							screenwriting instructor Robert McKee as “an exchange of behavior in action/reaction.” 
					

				

				 
					 
						 Those small pieces—the beats—build a scene... 
					

				

				 
					 
						 ...and scenes build an act. We analyze the division and subdivision of a story to
							understand what it’s about. 
					

				

				 
					 
						 And we find that we can do this with Ali Wong’s routine. Unlike some stand-up, it
							adds up into something bigger. She’s telling not just 100 individual jokes, but a story that is
							deliberately arranged, much like a comedy film or a TV series. 
					

				

				 
					 
						 We can think of comedy as a spectrum, from one-line jokes to a feature film. 
					

				

				 
					 
						 As we move from left to right, we have more topic continuity and use of structure.
							The humor requires and builds off of context. 
					

				

				 
					 
						 Ali Wong’s stand-up is closer to the right of this spectrum, relying less on
							one-liners and more on form-driven humor. It helps makes her routine great, and the jokes hit for
							different reasons than we sometimes expect in stand-up. The laughter climax is one example of this. 
					

				

				 
					 
						 Let’s zoom in again on the laughter climax to see
							why. 
					

				

				 
					 
						 We can tie this punchline to a larger three-minute story about making babies. 
					

				

				 
					 
						 It also “calls back” to three other topics from earlier in the routine. 
					

				

				 
					 
						 The laughter climax is meta funny. For 50 minutes, Ali has built a
							universe, with each joke expanding the audience’s understanding of her world-view. 
					

				

				 
					 
						 The laughter climax connects the major themes of her routine, from how she met her husband to her philosophy on
								working. When the punchline hits, the seemingly disparate stories snap together. 
					

				

				 
					 
						 You get the same feeling when reaching the end of a great Seinfeld episode or any
							multi-plot story—the delight in seeing all the plotlines converge into one (and realizing that the
							storyteller was crafting a deeper idea all along). 
					

				

				 
					 
						 Screenwriting educator Robert McKee devotes a large part of teaching
							to story structure. Screenwriting is not about the exact words said (i.e., the jokes) but the pattern of
							events and the meaning behind them. For example, here’s a point about structure that he makes in
							screenwriting bible Story ... 
					

				

				 
					 
						 “If, however, we were to put the content of their films aside for the moment, and
							study the pure patterning of their events, we’d see that, like a melody without a lyric, like a silhouette
							without a matrix, their story designs are powerfully charged with meaning.”
“Stripped of its surface of
							characterization and location, story structure reveals his personal insight into the deepest patterns and
							motivations for how and why things happen in this world––his map of life’s hidden order.” 
					

				

				 
					 
						 This is what we get when stand-up isn’t just joke after joke after joke. 
					

				

				 
					 
						 The structure of her routine leaves us with something more, much like a film short
							or a play would. Her hour-long show is different because we see her world-view. We understand her
							experience being pregnant. 
					

				

				 
					 
						 We learn Ali’s “map of life’s hidden order.”

content.thinking:
Good.

8. `making-babies-three-minutes`:
source: "We can tie this punchline to a larger three-minute story about making babies."
claim: "The 747-making babies topic spans 2846 to 3014 seconds, 168 seconds (2.8 minutes)."
code: `t[t.group=='747-making babies'][['group','timeStart','totalStop']].assign(seconds=lambda d: d.totalStop-d.timeStart, minutes=lambda d: (d.totalStop-d.timeStart)/60)`
Printout: 747-making babies 2846 3014 168 2.8. Good. But wait, is `totalStop` semantically the story's end? Row 102's totalStop=3014, yes. In general totalStop is "the end of the current top-level block". For 747-making babies, yes. The topic "747-making babies" starts at 2846 and the section ends at 3014. Note row 112 795-miscarriage totalStop 3149, so 3014 is parent pregnancy sub-block. Good.

9. `three-callbacks`:
source: "It also 'calls back' to three other topics from earlier in the routine."
claim: "The topic map has three callback annotations, pointing to earlier captions at 0:16:35, 0:4:46, and 0:44:24 from the 787-hippies, 805-mom, and 896-wet topics."
code: `t[t.callback.notna()][['group','timeStart','callback']]`
Printout:
110 787-hippies 2983 0:16:35
113 805-mom 3057 0:4:46
127 896-wet 3408 0:44:24
Claim numbers all appear (3 count from row count; names/timestamps). Good. Should we include? Maybe.

10. `not-100-jokes`? Skip (data description).

11. `three-minute-first`? Maybe no.

12. "50 minutes built universe" could be fact #1.

Now, do we include a fact about the "most laughter" being false? No, skipped.

But wait, maybe the story's chart actually labels the biggest laugh at 50:11 and the data's 11:48 is an error. If we skip the central finding, the task evaluator may expect it. Could we include a fact that reproduces "most laughter" by computing the max of laugh **within the final portion**? That would be cherry-picking a threshold, forbidden. Or compute max per topic? Max topic sum = 96-marriage 404, not 50:00. Max single line = 11:48. No.

Could "this moment" be the **punchline's cumulative laughter** (the last 5 lines of 789-conception): 0+0.75+2.5+0+2.5+9.5 = 15.25. Is that the max for any 24s span? Let's check exact max for a 24s window at each start—maybe 50:00's 24s is not max (we saw 20s window max 18.5 at 11:31). No.

Could "most laughter" mean **the largest single laugh in the second half**? 9.5 is max after 30 min? Let's check: line 686 at 43:17 has 8.5, 600 at 37:45 has 8.5, 710 at 45:09 7.0. So yes, 9.5 at 50:11 is the max in the second half. But story says entire show. Maybe they only analyzed the second half? No.

Could the 11:48 line's 10.0 be a **cumulative** overlap of simultaneous laughs, and the chart's circle at 50:11 bigger due to scaling? no.

I think skip with explanation is correct per instructions ("If ... the numbers differ beyond rounding, leave the finding out").

Now, are there chart labels we haven't captured that state more numbers? Let's try to get the page's SVG after render via microlink `data.html.selector=svg` once rate resets, or another service. Maybe the page uses SVG generated by D3, and microlink's body HTML would include it; it didn't—only text. Maybe visuals are in `<canvas>`. There may be `<div>` chart labels in body; we saw only words. So no numeric chart labels.

But the "Laughter Climax" section in the body (rendered) contains the punchline text only, no numbers. The "Pattern, Structure, Order" is empty placeholder. The charts are canvas.

Could the story have audio/annotations with numbers? no.

Let's consider that the expected facts might be based on the story's **visual** labels that we can't see, e.g., a timeline labeled "50:11" and "9.5 sec". We can still use the text quote.

Now let's verify fact codes with pandas and exact printouts. Also need to avoid numbers typed in code. Some code uses `t.level==1` — 1 is a category level, not a data-derived number; acceptable? "you never type a number into code" likely means don't hardcode results. Using `level==1` is a structural definition from the story's hierarchy. Fine. `t.group=='747-making babies'` is a name. `c.caption.str.contains(...)` is text. `t.group.str.contains('hpv')` is text. `.tail(1)` fine.

For the "three longest" claim, "three" is in the claim but code returns all six; the top three are visible. The claim says "three longest" and lists them; that's a ranking from the printout. Good.

For `three-callbacks`, the count "three" is not a printed number, just number of rows. The instruction says "every number... in the claim must be in the printout". Does row count count as printed? The printout has 3 rows but no explicit "3". We can add a column? Better code: `t[t.callback.notna()].assign(n_callbacks=lambda d: len(d))[['group','timeStart','callback','n_callbacks']]` — that's a bit hand-made but len is computed. Or use `.shape`? Printout of a DataFrame has "3 rows × 4 columns" in repr? Pandas `print(df)` doesn't show shape unless `info()`. The evaluate prints value the way pandas prints it. If the value is a DataFrame, its repr doesn't include row count. We can make the expression return a Series/DataFrame with a count column. Is `assign(n=lambda d: len(d))` acceptable? It's computing, not typing. But the instruction says "Do not assemble the result into a hand-made Series or dict." assign of a computed len is okay-ish. Alternative: `t.callback.notna().sum()` would print 3 but lose names/times. We could have two facts: one count (3) and one list. But the claim needs both count and names.

Maybe simpler: claim says "Three topics carry callback annotations: ..." and code returns a DataFrame with 3 rows. A reader sees three rows. Is that "in the printout"? Yes, implicitly. The instruction likely allows count from row count. Similar for HPV "three parts": three rows.

Could return a Series indexed by group with the callback as value: `t[t.callback.notna()].set_index('group').callback` → prints:
787-hippies    0:16:35
805-mom         0:4:46
896-wet         0:44:24
Three entries. Fine.

Let's now thoroughly validate all candidate facts and their printouts.

But first, let's reconsider the "three cohesive ideas" fact. The source says "structured around three cohesive ideas: getting older, marriage, and pregnancy." Our code prints the six level-1 topics, top three by duration. This reproduces the names and dominance. But is "level 1" the story's definition of cohesive ideas? The story's topic hierarchy has levels 1-6; level 1 is the top level. Yes, "levels" are described in the story's visualization? The text says "we analyze the division and subdivision of a story"; the data's levels. The level-1 topics include intro/paintball/conclusion, so saying "three cohesive ideas" = three longest top-level topics is an interpretation. But defensible: the three themes are the three longest.

Alternatively, use the group name prefixes? The level-1 groups with names "getting older", "marriage", "pregnancy" are exactly the story's three. Could filter level-1 groups excluding "intro", "paintball", "conclusion" by naming—not good. Ranking is cleaner.

Maybe the story's chart "Pregnancy, Marriage, Aging" labels the three themes with percentages of time. We could compute each as a share of the total. Let's decide whether to include shares. The claim should include only what code prints. We can print seconds and share:
`...assign(seconds=..., share=lambda d: d.seconds/c.timeStop.max())` but code references both tables; that's fine. Share of 3535 total. For marriage 52.1%, pregnancy 32.8%, getting older 10.2%. Would the story state those? Unknown. Don't add unstated numbers; claim can just rank and durations.

Wait—the claim must not include anything the printout does not show. If we claim "the three longest level-1 topics are marriage, pregnancy, and getting older, lasting 1840, 1160, and 361 seconds", printout shows. Good.

Now fact "making babies": 168 seconds and 2.8 minutes. Story says three-minute. Good. The claim "168 seconds (2.8 minutes)"—2.8 is printed by code. Good.

Now fact "climax 50 min": Claim "The 'I don't wanna work anymore' punchline is at 0:50:11 (50.2 minutes), drawing 9.5 seconds of laughter." Code prints minutes 50.183333; claim rounds 50.2, allowed. But "drawing 9.5 seconds of laughter" — the `laugh` column is the story's measure. Good.

However, note there are multiple "I don't wanna work anymore" lines; `.tail(1)` picks the last at 50:11. Is that the punchline the story shows? The story's Laughter Climax block ends with "'Cause I don't wanna work anymore." Yes. The last occurrence in the transcript is at 50:11. Good.

Now "climax is about conception": the topic 789-conception starts at 2990, but the punchline line at 3011 is within it. Code printing topic span. Good.

Now "orgasm→hippies→conception": The printout order if we don't sort is index order: 782-orgasm (index 109), 787-hippies (110), 789-conception (111). The timeStart values show 2956, 2983, 2990. Claim says conception starts at 2990 after hippies at 2983 after orgasm at 2956. Good. But "preceded by" could mean immediately previous topics; yes indices consecutive.

Now HPV facts. `t.group.str.contains('hpv')` matches 32-hpv, 39-men and hpv, 43-doctor and hpv. All lowercase? Yes. Case-sensitive 'hpv' appears in all. Good. Claim: "three topics ... spanning 154-230 seconds." The min timeStart 154, max topicEnd 230. Printout rows show 154 and 230; claim's "154-230" is computed by reader. Should we add a summary row? The claim's numbers appear. Fine. But "spanning 154-230" is a range; 154 is 32-hpv start, 230 is doctor end. Both in printout. Good.

Maybe claim "three topics: 32-hpv, 39-men and hpv, and 43-doctor and hpv" — exactly the rows. Great.

Now "sleep" fact: printout:
5 3 23-sleep 114 230
6 4 32-hpv 154 230
Claim "32-hpv (154-230) is nested inside 23-sleep (114-230): both end at 230 and HPV begins at 154." All numbers. Good.

Now "jealousy" fact: printout four rows with level. Claim "23-sleep (114-230) sits under 10-jealousy (62-230), alongside 16-metabolism (85-96) and 19-inner thigh clearance (96-111)." All in printout. Good.

Now "callbacks": include? Let's decide later after checking if the story's "three other topics" could be based on something else. Maybe we can find the original data's README online via GitHub search of the filename using grep.app? There's a code search service "grep.app" API. Try web_fetch https://grep.app/api/search?q=ali-wong--captions. This could find the repo and any analysis script with chart labels! Great idea.
